summary: Describes practices for operating DNS with security extensions, aimed at zone administrators deploying DNSSEC. It covers key generation, key storage, signature generation, key rollover, and related issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Locking a door is not enough; you need to take care of the keys. This memo gives tips for the people who run signed internet phone books.

questions: best practices for dnssec zone administrators
what is a ksk and zsk
subtitle: Practical advice for zone administrators on running DNSSEC: key roles, key rollovers, signature timing and NSEC or NSEC3.

tldr.problem: Signing a DNS zone is only the start. Keys have to be generated, stored, replaced and timed carefully, or validating resolvers mark the zone Bogus and its names can become invisible.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out the decisions a zone administrator faces and the choices for each: separate Key Signing Keys and Zone Signing Keys or not, Pre-Publish or Double-Signature rollovers, signature validity periods, and NSEC or NSEC3.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 4641. It says plainly that it is not 'Best Current Practices' and gives no strong recommendations.

facts.label: DS signature validity period suggested
facts.value: between a week and several months

today: RFC 6781 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 4641. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself says it is not 'Best Current Practices'.

sections.title: Scope and the Chain of Trust
sections.content:
RFC 6781 describes how to run a DNS zone that uses the DNS security extensions (DNSSEC). Its audience is zone owners, name server operators, registries, registrars and registrants. It focuses on serving authoritative data and assumes no direct relationship with the operators of validating recursive name servers.

The authors are careful about what the document is. At the time of writing there was still little production experience with DNSSEC below the top-level domain level, so the RFC says it should explicitly not be seen as 'Best Current Practices'. It describes the decisions, the available choices and some operational guidelines, and it gives no strong recommendations. Because it is operational advice and not a protocol specification, RFC 2119 requirement words do not apply to it.

The central idea is keeping the chain of trust intact. A broken chain makes data Bogus and can make whole subdomains invisible to verifying clients. Maintenance such as re-signing or key rollovers should be transparent to them. Published data also takes time to reach secondary servers and caches, so timing parameters matter.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a chain of people vouching for each other. If one link breaks, nobody trusts the answer at the end. The goal is to change keys without ever breaking a link.

sections.title: Key Roles, Storage and Strength
sections.content:
The DNSSEC validation protocol does not distinguish between kinds of keys; the split is purely operational. A Key Signing Key (KSK) signs only the DNSKEY set at the zone apex. A Zone Signing Key (ZSK) signs everything else. When one key does both jobs, the RFC calls it a Single-Type Signing Scheme. The split pays off because a ZSK can be replaced without involving the parent zone, while changing a KSK that the parent points to with a DS record, or that is configured as a trust anchor, involves third parties. By convention the SEP flag is set on KSKs, which makes the flags field an odd number. The flag plays no role in validation.

On effectivity periods, the RFC calls about one year reasonable for a KSK with a parent when an operator chooses regular rollovers, and a month reasonable for an online ZSK exposed to a fairly high risk. It describes three schools of thought for rolling a KSK that is not a trust anchor (regularly, frequently but irregularly, or only on suspected compromise) and says there is no widespread agreement on which is best.

For storage, the preference is to keep zone private keys and the master zone file on off-line, physically secure machines. Dynamic update forces at least one private key onto the master server or a hardware security module. A 'hidden master' arrangement can reduce that risk. The RFC suggests RSA/SHA-256 as the preferred signature algorithm at the time of writing, with RSA/SHA-1 as an alternative. It judges 1024-bit keys safe for most zones for at least the next ten years, and notes 2048 bits as the usual next size for higher-value keys.
sections.plainLanguage: It is smart to keep one master key locked in a safe and use a different everyday key for daily work. If the everyday key leaks, you swap it without bothering anyone else.

sections.title: Rolling and Replacing Keys
sections.content:
Rollovers are 'a fact of life' with DNSSEC, and the danger is caches. If a resolver holds data signed by an old key but not the old key itself, or the reverse, validation fails and the data is marked Bogus.

For a ZSK there are two schemes. In a Pre-Publish rollover the new key is published first, then signatures switch to it, then the old key is removed. This takes four stages and does not double the zone's signatures, but the new public key is exposed before use. In a Double-Signature rollover the zone is signed with both keys for a while, which takes three stages but doubles the number of signatures. For a KSK, only the key set is signed, so the double-signature approach has no zone-size cost, but it needs the parent to change the DS record and the child must wait for the old DS to expire from caches. The RFC also describes a Double-DS variant and says RFC 5011 style rollovers add a step where the old key is published with the REVOKE bit set.

Changing algorithms needs extra care, and the text describes a conservative and a liberal reading of RFC 4035. The RFC also covers emergencies. If a KSK is compromised, it advises not removing it before the parent has a DS record for the new KSK in place. A compromised ZSK is less severe because no parent interaction is needed. Stand-by keys published in advance can speed recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing a lock while people are still carrying old keys is tricky. You hand out new keys first, wait until everyone has them, and only then stop accepting the old ones.

sections.title: Parents, Operators and Signature Timing
sections.content:
A KSK change needs the parent. The RFC suggests that registry systems be able to store DS records, not just keys, because a child may use a digest algorithm the registry does not understand. It defines security lameness as the parent holding a DS record that points to a nonexistent DNSKEY. That is tolerable briefly during a Double-DS rollover, but if all DS records point nowhere, verifying clients mark the child Bogus. For the DS signature validity period it suggests something between a week and several months, as a compromise between child and parent.

When a registrant changes DNS operators, a cooperating losing operator can pre-publish the gaining operator's keys. If the losing operator will not cooperate, the only viable route is for the zone to go Insecure during the change, with the DS removed and later re-added. The RFC says there is no operational workaround for this business issue and that proper contracts seem to be the only solution.

Signatures add absolute time to the DNS. The RFC suggests the maximum zone TTL be smaller than the signature validity period, that re-signing happens well before expiry (a Refresh Period of a few days), and that the SOA expiration timer be about one third or a quarter of the signature validity period. It also warns that a minimum TTL under 5 to 10 minutes caused disruptions in workshop environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Signatures are like milk cartons with a use-by date. You must put fresh ones on the shelf well before the old ones run out, or the shop looks empty.

sections.title: NSEC or NSEC3
sections.content:
DNSSEC proves that a name does not exist by signing records that cover the gaps between existing names. There are two mechanisms. NSEC is a sorted list of names in clear text, which is simple and human readable but allows 'zone walking', where someone follows the list to read every name in the zone. NSEC3 hashes the names first, which makes walking harder. It does not stop leakage of the zone's size or which record types it holds.

The RFC says NSEC is preferred for highly structured zones such as in-addr.arpa., ip6.arpa. and e164.arpa., and for small zones with only a few guessable names, since hiding them is pointless there. NSEC3 is preferred for large zones where names are meant not to be readily available.

NSEC3 has tunable parameters. Iterations raise the cost of dictionary attacks: RFC 5155 gives limits of 150 for 1024-bit keys, 500 for 2048-bit keys and 2,500 for 4096-bit keys, and the RFC considers a value of 100 sufficiently costly yet not excessive. A changed salt makes an attacker lose precomputed work and needs no special rollover procedure. The Opt-Out flag lets a zone with mostly insecure delegations skip signing for them, and the RFC says it should be used only in such zones, typically large TLDs.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove a house number does not exist, you need a list of the real ones. A plain list can be read by anyone, and a scrambled list is harder to read but more work to make.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds data origin authentication and data integrity to the DNS using digital signatures over resource record sets. The RFC states that it does not protect against denial-of-service attacks and does not provide confidentiality.

The document's own concern is operational. Rolling keys takes time to propagate to verifying clients, and the data may be cached. Ignoring those propagation properties can cause validation failures because cached data does not match data fetched from the authoritative servers, which makes a secured zone unavailable to security-aware resolvers. For more general security considerations it points to RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing proves who wrote the answer and that nobody changed it, but it does not keep the answer secret. The biggest danger here is a slip-up while changing keys.

cells: Signatures are not doubled, but the new key is published early and exposed to cryptanalysis
Fewer stages, but the number of signatures in the zone doubles
Extra cost; does not hide zone size or record types
